Volume 15 · Chapter 03

Industrial organization and competition

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v15-c02

By the endAssess market conduct and competitive policy using models and evidence.

Capability and prerequisites

Assess pricing, entry, mergers and platforms by combining identified demand, explicit firm objectives and complete resource accounts. Prerequisite: labor economics and human capital; use the IV reasoning of instrumental variables and the equilibrium tools of games and strategic interaction. Every population and technology below is synthetic. The market-definition calculations are conditional economic diagnostics, not statements of any jurisdiction's current legal test.

What would actually change after the transaction?

Two suppliers propose to merge. Their customers dislike higher prices, their owners anticipate savings, and a prospective entrant promises to discipline the combined firm. A platform offers one group free access while charging another. These observations do not establish competitive harm or benefit. We need to know which customers substitute, who controls each price, which costs are real resources, and how entry and participation respond. Industrial organization connects those choices to evidence about particular markets.

A market share describes sales within a denominator; it does not identify a demand derivative or a counterfactual. Market power means an ability to profitably sustain a price above the relevant competitive benchmark in a specified environment. A markup can reflect differentiation, fixed-cost recovery or strategic conduct. Accounting gross margins do not automatically equal price minus economic marginal cost. Competition analysis therefore needs a mechanism and a measurement strategy, not just a concentration statistic.

Use five separate objects: preferences and substitution; technology and capacity; ownership and feasible actions; timing and information; and the welfare population. Changing ownership while holding demand and technology fixed is a meaningful experiment, but only a conditional one. A claim that a merger changes quality, innovation or costs requires additional evidence and an explicit channel. A before-and-after price difference mixes the transaction with every other contemporaneous change.

1. Demand slopes are not price–quantity correlations

Quantities q are units per market and prices p are numeraire goods per unit. In an interior two-product demand system write q=α−Dp+u, with vectors as columns. Positive diagonal entries of D give downward own-price demand; negative off-diagonal entries describe substitutes. The unobserved demand vector u may affect firms' pricing decisions. Centering all variables, the population regression coefficient matrix is Cov(q,p)Var(p)−1=−D+Cov(u,p)Var(p)−1. More observations estimate that association more precisely; they do not remove the second term.

An excluded shifter vector Z identifies unrestricted D through D=−Cov(q,Z)Cov(p,Z)−1 if E[uZ′]=0 and Cov(p,Z) has full rank. The first condition is exclusion plus orthogonality; the second is relevance in enough independent directions. A shifter named “cost” can also change quality, availability or customers' income. Its name supplies neither condition. With controls, apply the argument to properly residualized variables and defend the conditional moment restriction.

Salz's MIT demand lecture motivates the distinction between equilibrium price variation and preference parameters, and discusses instrument requirements and richer substitution models. Our finite population below isolates the identification issue without claiming to implement a random-coefficient demand estimator.

Worked case 1 — an endogenous price in every market

Set (α₁,α₂,D₁₁,D₁₂,D₂₁,D₂₂,p̄,s)=(20/3,20/3,4/3,−2/3,−2/3,4/3,6,1/4). Four independent equiprobable signs generate Z₁,Z₂,U₁,U₂∈{−s,s}. Let pᵢ=p̄+Zᵢ+Uᵢ and uᵢ=Uᵢ. There are sixteen equally weighted markets. This is a stipulated observational price process; it is not asserted to be the equilibrium pricing rule in case 2. Firms' information may include U even though the analyst does not observe it.

Independence gives (Var(pᵢ),Cov(Uᵢ,pᵢ),Cov(pᵢ,Zᵢ))=(1/8,1/16,1/16); every cross-product covariance with a different index is zero. Thus BOLS=[−5/6,2/3;2/3,−5/6], while BIV=[−4/3,2/3;2/3,−4/3]. Own-price sensitivity looks smaller under OLS because high demand raises both price and sales. Instruments recover the structural matrix here because the stipulated independent Z changes price without entering u.

All sixteen outcomes have strictly positive quantities: minimizing q₁=(20/3)−(4/3)(6+Z₁+U₁)+(2/3)(6+Z₂+U₂)+U₁ gives 8/3−1/3−1/12−1/6−1/6=23/12; symmetry gives the same lower bound for q₂. Consequently no censored-demand corner is hidden in the regression calculation. The population example contains no sampling uncertainty. An empirical implementation must additionally specify sampling, dependence across markets, weak-instrument diagnostics and uncertainty propagation to the merger counterfactual.

Demand estimation also requires a product universe and an outside option. Aggregating premium and basic versions can hide local substitution; ignoring a disappearing product can turn quality changes into apparent price responses. A credible application records quantities, transaction prices net of rebates, availability, ownership, characteristics and the time and geographic unit of observation. It checks whether estimates predict substitution in held-out episodes, not merely whether fitted sales resemble observed sales. Such checks can reject a model; agreement alone cannot prove exclusion.

2. Ownership changes the pricing derivative

For products owned by firm f, profit is Σj∈f(pⱼ−cⱼ)qⱼ(p), with constant marginal costs c. An interior optimum for pᵢ requires qᵢ+Σj∈f(pⱼ−cⱼ)∂qⱼ/∂pᵢ=0. Before a merger, a firm ignores profits diverted to the other owner. Afterwards those terms enter its objective. This local incentive is not itself the final price change: every controlled price must be reoptimized, with feasible demand and global optimality checked.

For a complete microfoundation, one consumer has numeraire wealth M and gross benefit G(q)=a(q₁+q₂)−(q₁²+q₂²+2γq₁q₂)/2, with q≥0 and 0≤γ<1. Utility is G(q)+x, where x=M−p·q≥0. The quadratic matrix B has diagonal 1 and off-diagonal γ. Since z′Bz=(1−γ)(z₁²+z₂²)+γ(z₁+z₂)²>0 for nonzero z, demand is unique. Where both quantities are positive, p=a1−Bq and qᵢ=[a(1−γ)−pᵢ+γpⱼ]/(1−γ²). At a zero quantity use the inequality a−qᵢ−γqⱼ−pᵢ≤0 instead of extrapolating negative purchases.

Worked case 2 — a merger and a real cost reduction

Take (a,γ,c,M,cefficient)=(10,1/2,4,100,2). Firms choose nonnegative prices simultaneously, then the consumer buys. Owners value numeraire profit; there are no other costs. Profit and consumer surplus receive equal weights in total surplus. The wealth constraint never binds: for unconstrained demand, p·q=aQ−q′Bq≤aQ−(1+γ)Q²/2≤a²/[2(1+γ)]=100/3<M. This bound also holds at corners because zero quantities contribute nothing to expenditure.

Separate firms satisfy 2pᵢ−γpⱼ=a(1−γ)+c. Hence (p₁,p₂,q₁,q₂)=(6,6,8/3,8/3). This is globally optimal against a rival price of 6: for 4≤pᵢ<8, profit is (pᵢ−4)(8−pᵢ)/(3/4), a strictly concave quadratic maximized at 6. Prices at least 8 sell nothing; below-cost prices earn negative profit because own demand is positive. They cannot improve on the strictly positive equilibrium profit.

There is no other equilibrium. Any price below 4 has positive own demand and a negative margin, so raising it to 4 improves profit. At prices at least 4 an inactive firm can earn positive profit by charging just above 4: even if its rival charged 4, its demand would remain positive. Thus both firms are active with positive margins. The two first-order equations are necessary; their unique solution is (6,6), already globally verified.

Consumer surplus equals q′Bq/2, since subtracting p·q from G cancels the linear term. Before merger, (CS,total profit,W)=(32/3,32/3,64/3). These are numeraire goods, not percentages. Transfers from consumer to owners enter opposite sides of the welfare account.

The merged owner's profit at any feasible demand is (a−c)(q₁+q₂)−q′Bq. Its Hessian −2B is negative definite. Maximization over all q≥0 therefore has the unique interior solution qᵢ=(a−c)/[2(1+γ)]. The implied nonnegative prices implement that optimum. This quantity argument bounds profit under every price vector, including demand corners, and establishes global pricing optimality. With unchanged cost, (p₁,p₂,q₁,q₂,CS,profit,W)=(7,7,2,2,6,12,18). The gain to the owner does not compensate the consumer loss in aggregate.

If a documented technological improvement reduces each marginal cost to 2, the merged optimum becomes (p₁,p₂,q₁,q₂,CS,profit,W)=(6,6,8/3,8/3,32/3,64/3,32). It uses fewer real resources at the same output. In this symmetric model merged price is (a+cnew)/2, so avoiding a price increase relative to 6 requires cnew≤2. An internal payment reclassification is not such an efficiency. Nor does the calculation prove that this reduction requires a merger rather than an available independent investment.

When using this framework, separate uncertainty about demand from uncertainty about conduct and efficiencies. Conditional on estimated demand, ownership and observed prices, a pricing equation may recover implied marginal costs; it does not independently verify the assumed pricing game. Compare implied costs with engineering or procurement evidence and test feasible alternative conduct assumptions. Large changes outside observed support require particular caution: functional form can dominate a precise-looking numerical prediction.

3. Entry creates benefits and consumes resources

Entry is a choice before competition, not a residual label for every new firm. Specify whether a cost is sunk before entry, avoidable by staying out, or incurred per unit afterwards. Also distinguish a planner selecting the number of firms while retaining market conduct from a planner controlling production. Berry and Waldfogel's entry study introduces the wedge from business taken from incumbents and the possible offset from lower prices or greater variety. We use that mechanism as context, not its radio-industry estimates.

Worked case 3 — profitable entry beyond the welfare-maximizing count

There are (potential firms,a,c,F)=(4,14,2,8). Firms first simultaneously choose entry. Entry consumes F units of real resources and is irreversible. After observing the entrant set, entrants simultaneously choose nonnegative quantities. Inverse demand is P(Q)=max{a−Q,0}. Owners receive sales revenue minus variable and entry costs. Consumers' gross benefit is the area under inverse demand; quantities considered below remain below the choke quantity.

For n≥1 entrants let A=a−c. Conditional on rivals' total R, producing where price is zero gives a strictly negative operating profit and is dominated by zero output. On the remaining range the payoff is q(A−R−q), so the best response is max{(A−R)/2,0}. At any equilibrium, if a firm produces positively its first-order condition gives A−Q=qᵢ>0. An inactive entrant would then have a positive marginal gain at zero. Thus all entrants produce, all qᵢ equal A−Q, and (qᵢ,Q,P,operating profit per firm) at n=3 =(3,9,5,9). In general qᵢ=A/(n+1), Q=nA/(n+1), and operating profit is A²/(n+1)². These best responses prove existence and uniqueness of each continuation, not just symmetry of a candidate.

An entrant must prefer its net profit to zero; an outsider must not gain by becoming the (n+1)st entrant. Thus A²/(n+1)²≥F and, when n<4, A²/(n+2)²≤F. Here the unique equilibrium count = 3: the third earns 9−8=1 and a fourth would earn 144/25−8<0. There are four corresponding identities of the excluded firm. This is a statement about pure equilibrium counts, not uniqueness of the entire simultaneous entry game including mixed strategies.

Welfare under the Cournot continuation is Wₙ=AQ−Q²/2−nF=A²[1−1/(n+1)²]/2−nF. Including no production at n=0, (W₀,W₁,W₂,W₃,W₄)=(0,46,48,87/2,928/25). A planner who can choose entry but must retain Cournot output chooses two firms. A planner also controlling production uses one plant and Q=A, because another identical plant adds only a fixed cost. Its (Q,W)=(12,64) differs from both the free-entry and constrained-planner allocations.

For entry from two to three firms, (entrant net gain,incumbents' combined loss,consumer gain,total change)=(1,−14,17/2,−9/2). The private entrant counts its own profit, not the incumbents' lost profit. Consumers gain from the lower price; fixed resources are nevertheless duplicated enough to reduce total welfare. Product variety, uncertainty, selection of better technologies and innovation are absent. Without evidence on those margins, this example does not recommend restricting actual entry.

4. A platform must attract both sides and pay its subsidies

A two-sided platform links groups whose participation affects the other group's willingness to join. A low fee on one side can increase receipts on the other. Rochet and Tirole's December 2002 manuscript analyzes price structure in two-sided markets. Their transaction model is not the membership game constructed here. The following fixed point and welfare accounts are derived for our stated primitives.

Worked case 4 — a negative fee with an explicit funding account

Each side has unit mass. A-types have direct value v uniformly distributed on [−1,0]; B-types have value uniformly on [0,1]. Joining gives v+αᵢnⱼ−fᵢ numeraire utility relative to staying out. Agents are nonatomic and take participation nⱼ as given. Let (αA,αB,owner reserve)=(1/4,3/4,1). The owner commits real-valued membership fees, then both sides choose whether to join with rational expectations. There is one platform, no alternative platform or multihoming, zero resource cost and no other externality. Agents have enough numeraire for positive fees. The owner receives profit and has the stated reserve before membership payments settle. Feasible contracts promise total gross subsidies no greater than that reserve even if everyone on a subsidized side joins; positive receipts need not arrive first.

Writing clip(z)=min{1,max{0,z}}, participation must satisfy nA=clip(αAnB−fA) and nB=clip(1+αBnA−fB). The map takes the unit square into itself and contracts sup-norm distances by at most 3/4, since clip never expands a distance. Starting anywhere, successive differences are bounded by a geometric sequence; the iterates are Cauchy in the closed square. Their limit is a fixed point by continuity. Two fixed points would have distance at most three quarters of itself, forcing equality. Thus fees induce one participation equilibrium even at boundaries.

Interior inverse fees are fA=αAnB−nA, fB=1+αBnA−nB. At full participation these formulas give the highest compatible fee. At zero participation its fee contributes zero receipts. Ignoring the reserve constraint for a moment, maximizing profit over all fees is equivalent to maximizing Π=nB−nA²−nB²+nAnB over the closed square. The Hessian has eigenvalues −1 and −3, so the stationary point is the unique global maximum.

Solving 2nA=nB and 2nB=1+nA gives (nA,nB,fA,fB)=(1/3,2/3,−1/6,7/12). The accounts are (A subsidy,B receipts,profit)=(1/18,7/18,1/3). The reserve of 1 covers even all A-types claiming their promised subsidy, which would cost only 1/6. Thus the unconstrained profit maximum is feasible under the reserve constraint, and is also the maximum over funded contracts. Negative fees require no unfunded transfer or reliance on collecting B fees first. The zero-cost assumption means profit is a transfer to the owner, not a resource loss.

Selected types on each side have aggregate net utility nᵢ²/2: integrate the distance of each participating value above its indifferent threshold. Hence (A surplus,B surplus,total welfare)=(1/18,2/9,11/18). Equivalently integrate direct values and add total network benefits: W=−nA²/2+nB−nB²/2+nAnB. This equals consumer surplus plus owner profit. Fees alone would mismeasure welfare because they cancel in the aggregate while network benefits do not.

Uniqueness here follows from the stated small cross effects. Stronger effects can create several self-consistent participation outcomes; a pricing prediction then needs an equilibrium selection or adjustment story. Platform market power cannot be judged solely from whether one side pays zero. Relevant evidence includes participation responses on both sides, the feasibility of switching and using several platforms, interoperability, congestion, quality, advertising exposure and who receives platform profit. Those mechanisms require extensions; the membership model does not silently include them.

5. Market definition is conditional on a baseline

A diversion ratio measures the fraction of lost sales of one product that moves to another after a specified change, locally or over a finite change. It depends on the experiment, product set and customers. A hypothetical joint price increase asks whether an owner of a proposed product group would profit by raising its prices, holding specified outsiders' actions fixed. It needs margins, demand responses and a baseline. This is useful substitution analysis even when no legal classification is being attempted.

For a common initial price p, constant unit cost c, markup share m=(p−c)/p>0, proportional price increase τ>0 and proportional aggregate sales loss L, the profit change is pQ[(m+τ)(1−L)−m]. Its sign is positive exactly when L<τ/(m+τ). This critical loss is a break-even calculation, not an estimate of actual sales lost. Fixed costs cancel only if unchanged; heterogeneous margins, changing costs or unequal price increases need product-level accounts.

Worked case 5 — the same goods, two baselines

Use case 2 with c=4 and (baseline price,proportional increase)=(6,1/10). Raising only p₁ to 33/5 gives (q₁,q₂,change in firm 1 profit)=(28/15,46/15,−12/25). Product 1 loses 4/5 unit and product 2 gains 2/5: diversion from 1 to 2 = 1/2. The unilateral increase is unprofitable because product 1's owner does not collect the other firm's gain.

If both products belong to the hypothetical owner and both prices rise to 33/5, each quantity is 34/15. Then (joint profit,profit change)=(884/75,28/25). The (single-product loss fraction,joint loss fraction,critical loss)=(3/10,3/20,3/13) explain the opposing results. One candidate fails this conditional profitability diagnostic and the pair passes it. Nothing here decides which legal market boundary an authority must adopt.

Now start at the already jointly optimal price 7 and raise both prices by the same percentage to 77/10. Each quantity becomes 23/15 and (joint profit,profit change)=(851/75,−49/75). The products and costs have not changed. The test fails because the baseline is already the joint owner's optimum. Inferring broad competition from this failure would mistake an elevated baseline for easy substitution. Baseline conduct must therefore be defended along with the demand estimate. Outsider reactions, entry and quality changes could also alter the experiment.

A usable competition memo separates the model result from the empirical claim. Report the product/customer scope and baseline date; identify the demand variation; document ownership and the decision horizon; distinguish verifiable marginal efficiencies from transfers; and calculate both consumer and total surplus where justified. Give a range across credible demand, conduct and entry assumptions. If a decision depends on an unmeasured network effect or efficiency, state the missing evidence and the value of resolving it. A precise answer to an unsupported model is not yet a precise answer to the policy question.

Exercises

  1. Replace Var(Uᵢ)=1/16 in case 1 by 3/16, retaining independence, Var(Zᵢ)=1/16 and pᵢ=6+Zᵢ+Uᵢ. Treat this as an uncensored linear statistical system. Derive the OLS matrix and IV identification. If only the common instrument Z₁+Z₂ is observed, identify exactly which combinations of the unrestricted demand slopes remain identified.
  2. In the original sixteen-market system add δZᵢ to the demand disturbance of equation i, leaving the price process unchanged. What matrix would the incorrectly excluded IV estimator recover? If δ∈[−1/5,1/5], give the identified interval for an own-price coefficient when the observed IV coefficient is −4/3. Explain why first-stage strength does not settle this sensitivity.
  3. In case 2 let the merged marginal cost be 3. Derive globally optimal prices, quantities, consumer surplus, profit and welfare. Compare consumer and total welfare with separate firms. State the resource assumption behind any gain.
  4. Keep separate owners but set (c₁,c₂)=(4,2). Derive the equilibrium prices and quantities and verify global unilateral optimality, including below-cost and zero-demand deviations.
  5. Set the entry cost in case 3 to F=9. List all pure-equilibrium entry counts, allowing indifference. Find the welfare-maximizing count when Cournot continuation is retained. Explain why a tie-breaking rule changes a selected outcome without changing the equilibrium inequalities.
  6. Reconstruct the entry-from-two-to-three welfare decomposition in case 3 using consumer surplus and firms' net profits separately. Prove that the unrestricted production planner uses one plant, rather than importing the constrained planner's choice of two.
  7. Swap the platform's cross effects to (αA,αB)=(3/4,1/4). Derive participation, fees and profit. Does the sign of A's fee reveal whether the profit-maximizing participation allocation changed? Then maximize total welfare over participation in the original case and explain the distinct objective.
  8. In a different platform model both sides have direct values uniform on [0,1], cross effect 2 and fee 3/2. Find every participation fixed point in the unit square. Explain precisely which step of case 4's uniqueness proof fails.
  9. Derive the general critical-loss formula. At the price-7 baseline in case 5, calculate the actual aggregate loss and critical loss for a ten-percent joint increase. Reconcile their comparison with the directly calculated profit change.
  10. Write a research plan to evaluate a proposed merger of two membership platforms. Specify the outcome and welfare population, data and identifying variation, ownership/participation counterfactual, entry horizon, subsidy funding, efficiency evidence and a falsifiable validation check. Explain why a pre/post price comparison on the paying side alone is insufficient. This is an open design question, not a request for an actual legal recommendation.
Full solutions and evaluation criteria
  1. Var(pᵢ)=1/4 and Cov(Uᵢ,pᵢ)=3/16, so the bias is (3/4)I. Thus BOLS=[−7/12,2/3;2/3,−7/12]. With both Z variables, Cov(p,Z)=(1/16)I remains invertible and orthogonality still identifies −D. With the scalar common instrument, Cov(p,Z₁+Z₂)=(1/16,1/16)′. Each equation identifies only its sum of price coefficients. Adding any row (t,−t) leaves that moment unchanged; this explicitly constructs nonidentification of the individual coefficients. Extra symmetry or diagonal restrictions would be extra identifying assumptions, not a consequence of the scalar instrument.
  2. Now Cov(u,Z)=δ(1/16)I, so the coefficient estimate is −D+δI, or the reported D estimate is D−δI. If the observed own-price coefficient is −4/3, the true coefficient equals −4/3−δ and therefore lies in [−23/15,−17/15]. Off-diagonal coefficients remain unchanged under this particular violation. The first stage is exactly the original full-rank matrix for every δ. Relevance cannot test the direct demand channel; a narrower interval needs a substantive exclusion bound or another valid source of variation.
  3. The merged quantity objective has Hessian −2B regardless of c, so its stationary point is globally optimal. Substituting c=3 gives (p₁,p₂,q₁,q₂,CS,profit,W)=(13/2,13/2,7/3,7/3,49/6,49/3,49/2). Consumer surplus changes by −5/2, whereas total welfare rises by 19/6 relative to 64/3. The lower real marginal input requirement can improve aggregate welfare while the higher price harms consumers. This comparison assumes a real cost reduction for every produced unit; neither a transfer within the merged organization nor an unverified accounting saving establishes it.
  4. The equations are 2p₁−p₂/2=9 and 2p₂−p₁/2=7. Therefore (p₁,p₂,q₁,q₂)=(86/15,74/15,104/45,176/45). Quantities also satisfy qᵢ=(4/3)(pᵢ−cᵢ). Against p₂=74/15, the rival remains active whenever p₁≥c₁=4: the threshold below which product 2 would disappear is 2p₂−10=−2/15. Against p₁=86/15, product 1 remains active whenever p₂≥2 because its disappearance threshold is 22/15<2. In each case the own positive-demand branch is a strictly concave profit quadratic with its maximizer at the computed price; above its choke price profit is zero. At any own price below cost, own demand is positive and profit negative. Thus every feasible unilateral price deviation is covered. The same no-inactive-firm argument applies since even a price just above each cost leaves positive residual demand at the rival's cost; the interior linear equations then imply uniqueness.
  5. For n=2 operating profit is 16≥9 and a third would earn 9=F. For n=3 each earns 9=F and a fourth earns 144/25<9. Neither n=1 nor n=4 satisfies both conditions; n=0 admits profitable entry. Thus the pure counts are (2,3). Welfare subtracts one extra resource unit per entrant from case 3: (W₀,W₁,W₂,W₃,W₄)=(0,45,46,81/2,828/25), so two is uniquely best under Cournot continuation. An entrant indifferent between entering and staying out may do either in Nash equilibrium. A specified rule against zero net gains selects two; it does not justify replacing weak inequalities in the unrefined game.
  6. At n=2, Q=8, consumer surplus Q²/2=32 and each firm's net profit is 16−8=8. At n=3, Q=9, consumer surplus is 81/2 and each net profit is 1. Consumers gain 17/2; the two original firms together lose 14; the new owner gains 1. Sum −9/2 agrees with 87/2−48. For a full planner, given any Q>0, one plant can produce the entire quantity at the same variable cost as several. Every additional plant wastes F>0 without capacity or variety benefit. With one plant maximize 12Q−Q²/2−8 on 0≤Q≤14; the strict concave maximum is Q=12 and W=64. For Q>14 gross benefit stops increasing while production costs rise, so that region cannot improve the solution. Not producing yields zero, also inferior.
  7. The sum of cross effects stays one, leaving the participation profit quadratic unchanged. The contraction bound remains 3/4. Hence (nA,nB,fA,fB,profit)=(1/3,2/3,1/6,5/12,1/3). Fee incidence changes while the allocation and profit do not. In the original welfare problem W=nB−(nA−nB)²/2≤nB≤1; equality requires nA=nB=1. Thus the full-participation planner obtains W=1. Original inverse fees (−3/4,3/4) implement that allocation with zero platform profit and balanced membership transfers; reserve 1 also covers the gross subsidy 3/4. The private owner instead chooses participation to maximize receipts, ignoring surplus accruing to participants.
  8. The equations are nA=clip(2nB−1/2) and its symmetric counterpart. If one coordinate is zero, the other must be zero; if one is one, the other must be one. Otherwise both are interior; subtracting the linear equations yields 3(nA−nB)=0 and substitution gives n=1/2. The complete list is [(0,0),(1/2,1/2),(1,1)]. The map is continuous and maps the square to itself, but its Lipschitz bound 2 is not below one. The inequality d≤2d permits a positive distance and cannot prove uniqueness. The middle equilibrium's instability under simultaneous iteration is a separate adjustment property, not a reason to erase it from the rational-expectations equilibrium set.
  9. Initial variable profit is (p−c)Q=pQm. New profit is [p(1+τ)−c]Q(1−L)=pQ(m+τ)(1−L). Subtract, divide by positive pQ(m+τ), and obtain L<τ/(m+τ); equality gives unchanged profit. At p=7, m=3/7 and τ=1/10, so critical loss is 7/37. Quantities fall from 2 to 23/15 per product, making actual loss 7/30. Thus (actual loss,critical loss)=(7/30,7/37). Actual loss exceeds the threshold, consistent with −49/75 profit change. The direction differs from the price-6 baseline because both the starting margin and the sales response differ; substituting one baseline's margin into the other's quantity calculation would mix experiments.
  10. A complete answer defines the customer groups, products, dates and owner population; measures net fees, participation, usage, switching, service quality and costs on both sides; and states an outcome such as compensating variation under an explicitly estimated utility model. An illustrative design uses independently timed input-price changes affecting one platform's cost but not users' direct values, defends exclusion against quality adjustment, and checks that the resulting fee variation identifies both own and cross-side responses. It then solves the ownership counterfactual with a declared participation equilibrium selection, endogenous fees, feasible subsidy reserves and an entry horizon consistent with observed setup times. Efficiency evidence should identify real marginal resource savings and why another arrangement cannot achieve them. A held-out cost episode can test predicted substitution and participation; a failure requires revising or narrowing the model. Pre/post paying-side fees alone confound common demand shocks, altered quality and composition, and omit the subsidized side and owner receipts. Evaluate answers for these explicit objects and credible threats/remedies, not for whether they favor the merger. Alternative experimental or quasi-experimental designs are acceptable when their estimand and extrapolation limits are defended.

Teach-back, delayed retention and extension

Teach a colleague why an observed markup, a profitable merger and a welfare-improving merger are three different claims. Use case 2 to show the owner gain without efficiency, then exercise 3 to show consumer harm alongside a total surplus gain. State what would have to be measured before applying either result.

After one week, without notes: reconstruct the IV bias term; derive the ownership pricing condition; write both entry inequalities including ties; explain how the platform subsidy is funded; and diagnose the price-7 baseline failure. The answer keys are respectively Cov(u,p)Var(p)−1, the sum over commonly owned products, weak entrant/nonentrant profit inequalities, a prefunded reserve plus membership receipts, and testing above an already optimal joint price. After one month, change one assumption in each mechanism and identify which proof step survives. Merely recalling the numerical answers does not demonstrate transfer.

Further study should extend demand heterogeneity and identification, dynamic entry and investment, bargaining in vertical relationships, and platform competition with multihoming. The sources support the bounded method context cited above. The five cases and ten exercises are original derivations, not reproduced empirical estimates or legal guidance.

Sources and further study

  • Tobias Salz, Introduction to Empirical Models of Demand, MIT 14.271 Lecture 07 (Fall 2022) — Price endogeneity, instrument rank/exclusion and demand substitution method context.
  • Steven Berry and Joel Waldfogel, Free Entry and Social Inefficiency in Radio Broadcasting, NBER Working Paper5528 (April1996) — Business-stealing wedge and offsetting price/variety benefits as entry context only.
  • Jean-Charles Rochet and Jean Tirole, Platform Competition in Two-Sided Markets, December13,2002 manuscript — Cross-side participation and platform price-structure context.
